# Register Allocation, Loop Vectorization, and Instruction Scheduling: A Technical Deep-Dive

## 1. Register Allocation

Register allocation maps an unbounded set of virtual registers (program variables/temporaries) onto a finite set of physical registers, inserting spill code (loads/stores to memory) when the demand exceeds supply. The central correctness invariant is that two virtual registers simultaneously live (interfering) must never be assigned the same physical register, and spill/reload code must preserve program semantics exactly at the points of insertion.

**Graph-coloring register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs style).** The classical formulation, originating with Chaitin et al. and refined by Briggs, Cooper, Kennedy, and Torczon, builds an interference graph where nodes are virtual registers (or, in the "live range" formulation, maximal live ranges) and edges connect pairs that are simultaneously live at some program point. A k-coloring of this graph, where k is the number of available physical registers, corresponds to a valid allocation; graph coloring is NP-complete in general, so the allocator uses heuristics rather than exact algorithms. The Chaitin algorithm uses Kempe's simplification rule: repeatedly remove nodes of degree < k (such a node can always be colored after its neighbors, since fewer than k colors are forbidden), pushing removed nodes onto a stack. If no such node exists, a node is chosen for optimistic spilling based on a spill cost heuristic, typically the ratio of estimated dynamic use/def weight (loop-nesting-depth-scaled) to the node's degree, favoring cheap-to-spill, high-degree nodes. After simplification, nodes are popped and colored; a node that fails to find a free color at this stage is actually spilled (Briggs introduced "optimistic coloring," deferring the spill decision to the select phase rather than committing at simplify time, often reducing unnecessary spills). Spilled live ranges are rewritten with explicit loads/stores around each use/def, new virtual registers are introduced for the spilled values, and the whole process iterates to a fixed point. Complexity is dominated by interference graph construction, O(n²) or better with sparse bitset representations over live ranges, and the iterative spill-rewrite loop in the worst case re-executes coloring multiple times, though in practice this converges quickly. **Coalescing** merges the nodes of a MOVE instruction's source and destination when they don't interfere, eliminating the move; naive coalescing can inadvertently increase graph degree past k, provoking extra spills. Chaitin's original coalescing is aggressive (always coalesce if non-interfering) and can harm colorability. Briggs coalescing is conservative: a merge is permitted only if the resulting merged node has fewer than k neighbors of significant degree (degree ≥ k), guaranteeing colorability is preserved. George coalescing offers an intermediate, asymmetric safety test. These safety conditions are essential correctness properties, not just heuristics—unsafe coalescing can make a colorable graph uncolorable, forcing unnecessary (but not incorrect) spills; it never causes miscompilation but can regress performance severely if violated carelessly in combination with assumptions elsewhere in the allocator.

**Linear scan register allocation (Poletto & Sarkar).** Designed for JIT and other compile-time-sensitive contexts, linear scan abandons full interference-graph construction in favor of computing live intervals: for each virtual register, a single contiguous range (or small set of ranges, in extended versions) from first definition to last use, under the assumption that the program is processed in some linear order (commonly a linearization of basic blocks consistent with control flow, though this is an approximation since live intervals computed this way are supersets of true liveness in the presence of complex control flow). Intervals are sorted by start point and scanned left to right using an active set of currently-live intervals; a register is assigned from the free pool, and when register pressure exceeds capacity, the interval with the furthest-away next use (or, in the simplest form, highest end point) is spilled. Complexity is O(n log n) for sorting plus near-linear scan work, dramatically faster than graph coloring's effectively higher-order behavior, which is why linear scan is the dominant allocator in JITs (e.g., early HotSpot client compiler, LLVM's fast register allocator path, V8's prior allocators). The precision/speed tradeoff is explicit: linear scan's single-interval approximation of liveness is coarser than true graph coloring, producing measurably more spills and more missed coalescing opportunities on CPU-bound ahead-of-time code, but its near-linear complexity and simple data structures make it attractive when compilation latency matters more than peak code quality. Correctness hinges on accurate interval computation (conservative over-approximation of liveness is safe; under-approximation is not) and correct spill-code placement at interval boundaries consistent with control-flow edges.

**SSA-based register allocation (Hack, Grund, Goos et al.).** This approach exploits a key structural property: the interference graph of a program in strict SSA form is a **chordal graph** (every cycle of length ≥ 4 has a chord), because live ranges in SSA correspond to subtrees of the dominator tree intersected with specific CFG structure, and chordal graphs are colorable optimally in polynomial time via simplicial elimination ordering (perfect elimination ordering), with greedy coloring along that ordering guaranteed optimal — no NP-completeness obstacle arises. The SSA-based allocator separates the problem cleanly into: (1) spilling, decided by a separate heuristic or an optimal spilling formulation (sometimes posed as an integer program or belady-style furthest-first heuristic adapted to SSA liveness), (2) coloring, done optimally and quickly on the chordal graph via the perfect elimination ordering derived from a structure like the dominance tree combined with block order, and (3) a final **SSA deconstruction (out-of-SSA translation)** phase that inserts copies to resolve phi-nodes, which is itself where coalescing-like copy minimization is applied, since naive phi resolution introduces many physical-register copies at block boundaries. The complexity advantage is coloring in polynomial time (linear in practice) rather than relying on heuristic simplify/spill iteration; the main engineering cost shifts to the SSA-destruction copy-insertion/coalescing step. Correctness considerations center on precise SSA liveness computation (dominance-based live-range intersection must be exact) and on ensuring phi-elimination copies are inserted on the correct CFG edges (using edge splitting to avoid the "lost copy" and "swap" problems when parallel copies at a join point have cyclic dependencies).

**Spilling and rematerialization.** Spilling inserts store instructions after definitions and load instructions before uses of the spilled live range, splitting it into shorter sub-ranges; correctness requires that the inserted memory location is not aliased or clobbered and that insertion points are placed on every path where the value is live, including SSA phi-related control paths. Rematerialization is an alternative to spilling to memory: if a value's defining computation is cheap and side-effect-free (e.g., a constant load, address computation, or simple arithmetic from still-live operands), the compiler recomputes the value at the use point instead of reloading from a spill slot, avoiding memory traffic at the cost of redundant computation; correctness requires verifying that all operands of the rematerialized instruction remain unmodified and available at the new recomputation point, which is a conservative dataflow condition.

**Register-pressure-aware scheduling/allocation interaction.** List schedulers that reorder instructions for ILP can increase live-range overlap and thus register pressure, counteracting the allocator; pressure-sensitive scheduling heuristics (e.g., preferring to schedule consumers soon after producers to shorten live ranges, or integrating a pressure-tracking heuristic such as the "register pressure" priority function in LLVM's scheduler) mediate this by estimating, at each scheduling decision, the number of live values crossing the current point and penalizing choices that would exceed the target's physical register count, since a scheduling decision made in ignorance of allocation can force otherwise-avoidable spills — this is fundamentally a phase-ordering problem between scheduling and allocation with no universally optimal resolution, addressed in practice by either pre-allocation pressure-aware scheduling, post-allocation scheduling (scheduling after registers are fixed, sacrificing some ILP opportunity), or integrated approaches that interleave the two.

## 2. Loop Vectorization

Loop vectorization transforms scalar loop iterations into operations over SIMD vector registers, executing multiple logical iterations per vector instruction. Its soundness rests entirely on dependence analysis establishing that reordering/batching iterations preserves the original program's observable behavior.

**Classic loop-level vectorization with dependence-based legality checks.** The traditional (Allen-Kennedy style) vectorizer analyzes array-subscript dependences across loop iterations using **distance vectors** and **direction vectors**. For a pair of array accesses in a loop nest, the dependence distance is the difference in iteration indices at which the same memory location is touched; a direction vector records whether the dependence is "<", "=", or ">" along each loop dimension. A loop is **vectorizable at a given loop level** if there is no loop-carried true dependence (flow dependence) with a direction "<" at that level that would require values produced in one SIMD lane to be consumed by an earlier-executing lane within the same vector operation — concretely, if the dependence distance along the candidate vectorized dimension is zero (no cross-iteration dependence) or the direction is uniformly "=" (dependence only within an iteration, not across), vectorization is legal; a backward loop-carried dependence (direction ">") within the vectorized dimension, meaning iteration i+1 depends on iteration i's result, is generally illegal without transformation (though a uniform dependence distance ≥ vector length can still be vectorized safely, since no overlap occurs within a single vector width). Reduction operations (sum, max, etc.) create an apparent self-dependence that is specially recognized and handled by reduction idiom detection, which rewrites the reduction into a partial-vector-accumulate followed by a horizontal reduction at loop exit, rather than treating it as a blocking dependence. Trip-count-based legality additionally requires either a compile-time-known trip count divisible by the vector length or a generated remainder/epilogue loop (scalar cleanup loop) to handle the non-multiple remainder.

**SLP (Superword-Level Parallelism) vectorization (Larsen & Amarasinghe).** Unlike loop-level vectorization, which looks for parallelism across loop iterations, SLP vectorization finds parallelism within straight-line code (a single basic block, or unrolled loop body) by identifying groups of isomorphic, independent scalar instructions that can be packed into a single SIMD instruction. The algorithm starts from "seed" pairs — typically adjacent memory accesses (e.g., consecutive array loads/stores) — and grows packs transitively by following the use-def and def-use chains: if two instructions are isomorphic (same opcode, compatible types) and their corresponding operands are either already packed or can themselves be packed, they are combined. This produces a set of "PackSet" groups; code generation then replaces each pack with one vector instruction, inserting pack/unpack (shuffle) instructions at pack boundaries where scalar and vector values interact. SLP's legality condition is simpler than loop-level dependence analysis in one sense — no loop-carried dependence reasoning is required, since the targeted code is already straight-line — but still requires independence between the packed operations (no overlapping memory writes among the instructions being fused) and correct handling of memory alignment and potential aliasing between the packed loads/stores. SLP is widely used in LLVM and GCC specifically to vectorize unrolled loop bodies and straight-line kernels that classic loop vectorization structurally cannot address, and is often applied as a complementary pass after loop unrolling or alongside loop vectorization.

**Loop versioning, runtime alias checks, and masked/predicated vectorization.** When static dependence analysis cannot prove independence at compile time, most commonly due to pointer-based array accesses whose aliasing relationship is unknown (e.g., `a[i] = b[i] + c[i]` where a, b, c are raw pointers), the compiler emits **loop versioning**: a runtime check comparing the pointer ranges (e.g., verifying that [a, a+n) does not overlap [b, b+n) or [c, c+n)) selects, at runtime, between a vectorized version (executed when ranges are proven disjoint for this invocation) and a safe scalar fallback version. This converts a static-legality problem into a dynamic guard, trading a runtime branch and comparison for broadened applicability. Separately, the **remainder/epilogue loop** problem — handling a trip count not evenly divisible by the vector width — is addressed either by a scalar epilogue loop that executes the leftover iterations one at a time, or by **masked/predicated vectorization**, where a vector mask (predicate register, as in AVX-512's k-registers or ARM SVE's predicate registers) disables lanes corresponding to out-of-range iterations, allowing a single vectorized loop body to handle the full iteration space including the tail without a separate scalar loop. Predicated vectorization additionally supports vectorizing loops with conditional control flow inside the loop body (if-conversion): branches are converted to data-dependent predicates, and select/masked-store instructions replace control-flow-guarded stores. Vector cost modeling then decides, per target ISA (e.g., AVX2's 256-bit registers vs. AVX-512's 512-bit registers and native masking vs. SVE's scalable vector length and first-class predication), whether the estimated cost of the vectorized version — accounting for pack/unpack shuffle overhead, gather/scatter cost for non-contiguous accesses, and mask management overhead — is lower than the scalar version's cost; this is where architecture-specific instruction selection (choosing between full SIMD lane-width operations, masked variants, or gather/scatter intrinsics) is finalized based on the target's actual instruction set and its measured or modeled throughput/latency characteristics.

## 3. Instruction Scheduling

Instruction scheduling reorders instructions within a scheduling region to maximize instruction-level parallelism (ILP), hiding latency and avoiding pipeline stalls, subject to preserving all true data dependences, avoiding resource conflicts, and respecting control dependences.

**List scheduling.** The dominant basic-block scheduling technique builds a data-dependence DAG where nodes are instructions and edges represent dependences: true/flow dependences (read-after-write, RAW), anti-dependences (write-after-read, WAR), and output dependences (write-after-write, WAW) — the latter two being name dependences that can often be eliminated via register renaming rather than enforced by ordering. Each instruction is annotated with a priority, commonly the length of the longest path from that instruction to the end of the DAG (the **critical path** heuristic), since instructions on the critical path should be scheduled as early as slack allows to avoid extending the overall schedule length. The algorithm maintains a "ready list" of instructions whose dependence predecessors have already been scheduled, and at each cycle selects the highest-priority ready instruction (subject to resource/functional-unit availability, modeled via a reservation-table or resource-vector check), simulating machine resource occupancy as it goes. Complexity is roughly O(n²) for DAG construction plus O(n log n) for priority-queue-driven selection in common implementations. Correctness requires that no reordering violates a true dependence (RAW) — since violating this changes a value actually consumed — while WAR/WAW hazards can be legally reordered if renaming is applied, or must otherwise be respected as ordering constraints if the underlying register/memory location cannot be renamed. Resource conflicts (two instructions both needing the same functional unit/port in the same cycle) are handled by the reservation-table check refusing to issue a second instruction into an occupied resource slot in a given cycle.

**Trace scheduling.** To extract ILP beyond single-basic-block boundaries, trace scheduling (Fisher) selects a "trace" — a frequently executed, probable path (determined via profile data or heuristic branch prediction) spanning multiple basic blocks and possibly jumping over branches — and schedules it as if it were a single large block, hoisting instructions across branch boundaries including speculatively moving instructions above a branch into the trace before the branch is resolved. Because this speculative motion can place instructions on the trace's main path that would not have executed on an off-trace path (or vice versa, delay instructions that were needed off-trace), the technique requires **compensation code**: copies of instructions inserted on the off-trace (side-entrance/side-exit) edges to restore correct semantics for control flow that diverges from the chosen trace. This compensation code insertion is the crux of trace scheduling's correctness: every off-trace path must still compute the same values and side effects as the unscheduled program, which can cause significant code growth if traces are chosen poorly or if many side exits require duplicated compensation instructions; profile guidance is used precisely to minimize the frequency with which the (more expensive, now compensation-laden) off-trace paths are actually taken.

**Software pipelining via modulo scheduling.** For loops, software pipelining overlaps the execution of successive loop iterations so that each pipeline stage of iteration i+1 begins before iteration i completes, rather than scheduling only within one iteration. **Modulo scheduling** is the standard formulation: it schedules a single loop iteration's instructions into a compact "kernel" schedule of length equal to the **initiation interval (II)**, the number of cycles between the start of successive iterations, such that the kernel, when repeated every II cycles, produces a legal overlapped execution; the surrounding **prologue** (ramp-up) and **epilogue** (ramp-down) code handle the partial overlap at loop entry and exit. The **minimum initiation interval (MII)** is computed as the maximum of two lower bounds: the **resource-constrained MII (ResMII)**, derived from the most heavily used functional unit's total demand divided by its availability per cycle (if a resource is needed k times per iteration and the machine has p units of that resource, ResMII ≥ ⌈k/p⌉), and the **recurrence-constrained MII (RecMII)**, derived from the loop's dependence cycles (loop-carried dependences): for each cycle in the dependence graph with total latency L and total dependence distance D (number of iterations spanned), RecMII ≥ ⌈L/D⌉, and the overall RecMII is the maximum over all such cycles, since a cyclic dependence that spans D iterations and takes L cycles to resolve cannot be scheduled tighter than that ratio without violating the recurrence. The actual II used is typically found by starting at MII = max(ResMII, RecMII) and incrementally attempting to construct a legal modulo schedule (often via modulo-variable-expansion-aware list scheduling with backtracking), increasing II if no legal schedule is found at the current value. Correctness requires that the modulo-scheduled kernel's resource usage, when wrapped into any register's lifetime spanning more than one II, is handled by either modulo variable expansion (unrolling the kernel enough times that no physical register is required to hold more than one value's lifetime simultaneously) or dedicated rotating register files (as in some VLIW/EPIC architectures) to avoid incorrect overwriting of a value still live from a prior overlapped iteration.

**Region scheduling / superblock scheduling.** An alternative to full trace scheduling that avoids the complexity of general compensation code, superblock scheduling restricts the scheduling region to a single-entry, multiple-exit sequence of basic blocks (a superblock), constructed by **tail duplication**: whenever a block with multiple incoming edges would otherwise sit in the middle of a desirable scheduling region, it is duplicated so that each predecessor gets its own private copy, guaranteeing the region has exactly one entry point. This eliminates the need for the general side-entrance compensation code that trace scheduling requires (since there are no side entrances into a superblock by construction), while still permitting speculative code motion across the internal block boundaries within the superblock and across its multiple side exits (early-exit branches), with correctness maintained by ensuring that instructions speculatively hoisted above a conditional branch do not have side effects that would be incorrect if the branch is actually taken to exit early — handled either by restricting speculation to side-effect-free, non-trapping instructions or by inserting compensation code at the (now limited, duplication-free) side exits. Region/superblock scheduling is widely used in practice (e.g., in the IMPACT compiler and subsequent VLIW/EPIC toolchains) as a pragmatic middle ground between single-basic-block list scheduling's limited ILP window and trace scheduling's compensation-code complexity.
